files.content:
Shelf Life — Episode 12 raw transcript (auto-generated, unedited)
Recorded 2026-07-09. Host: Noor. Guests: Marta Velde (bookbinder), Daan Pols (apprentice).

[00:00] NOOR: Welcome back to Shelf Life. Today we are in an actual bindery, which smells like glue and paper dust and, honestly, like heaven.
[00:42] NOOR: Marta Velde has been binding books by hand for thirty-one years. Marta, welcome.
[01:15] MARTA: Thank you. You are the first person to bring a microphone in here. Usually they bring broken books.
[02:30] NOOR: Let's start there. What arrives on your bench in an average week?
[03:48] MARTA: Family bibles, mostly. And cookbooks. People cry over cookbooks more than bibles, if you want the truth. The stains are the memories.
[05:10] NOOR: How did you learn the trade?
[06:55] MARTA: My teacher took me on in 1995. Four years sweeping floors before he let me sew a spine. I tell people that and they think it is cruelty. It was patience.
[08:20] NOOR: And now you have an apprentice of your own. Daan, you are twenty-three. Why this trade?
[09:45] DAAN: I was studying logistics and I hated every minute of it. I saw Marta repair a 1911 atlas on a video and I emailed her that night.
[11:02] MARTA: He emailed me eleven times.
[12:30] NOOR: Persistence is the trade, from what I am hearing. Marta, walk me through the atlas repair. What does a book like that need?
[14:05] MARTA: First you take it apart completely. People are shocked by that. To save a book you must be willing to reduce it to sheets and thread.
[15:40] MARTA: The spine linings come off with wheat starch paste and a bone folder. Slow. If you rush the paste you tear the paper and then you are not a binder, you are a butcher.
[17:12] NOOR: How long does a full rebind take?
[18:50] MARTA: Twenty hours for a simple case binding. The atlas took ninety. We charge less than the hours, always. Nobody pays what the hours cost. You do it because the book deserves it.
[20:15] NOOR: Daan, what is the hardest skill so far?
[21:48] DAAN: Sewing headbands. Marta makes it look like knitting. Mine look like a fishing accident.
[23:30] NOOR: For listeners who want to try this — where do they start?
[25:05] MARTA: We teach beginner classes at the bindery, first Saturday of every month. The schedule is at bindery-lane.example.com/classes.
[26:40] NOOR: I will put that in the shownotes. What about materials? People always ask where to buy proper paper.
[28:15] DAAN: Paper Road. It is a small mill shop, they ship everywhere. paperroad.example.org. Their 90-gram laid paper is what we sew practice blocks with.
[29:50] NOOR: And if someone has a family book that needs repair but you are booked out?
[31:20] MARTA: The guild keeps a directory of certified binders by region — guild-of-binders.example.net/directory. Anyone listed there will treat your book honestly.
[33:00] NOOR: What is a book you refused to repair?
[34:35] MARTA: A first edition someone wanted rebound in neon leather. I sent them away. Restoration is listening to the book, not shouting over it.
[36:10] NOOR: Daan, where do you want to be in ten years?
[37:45] DAAN: Running my own bench. Maybe here. Marta says the bindery outlives the binder, and I want that to be true.
[39:20] MARTA: It is true. This bench was my teacher's bench. The scars in the wood are his.
[40:55] NOOR: That gave me chills. Before we close — the mailbag question. A listener asks: are e-readers killing your trade?
[42:30] MARTA: The opposite. The rarer the physical book becomes, the more the surviving ones matter. My waiting list has never been longer.
[44:05] NOOR: Marta Velde, Daan Pols, thank you both. Come back with the apprentice's first solo binding.
[45:40] DAAN: Deal. Give me a year.
[46:52] NOOR: Shelf Life is back Monday. Bring us your broken cookbooks.
[47:30] END OF RECORDING
